{{Short description|Mathematical model of crack growth}}
[[File:Gilbert tessellation.svg|thumb|A Gilbert tessellation]]
[[File:Gilbert tessellation axis.svg|thumb|Gilbert tesselation with axis-parallel cracks]]
In [[applied mathematics]], a '''Gilbert tessellation'''<ref name="ss10">{{citation
 | last1 = Schreiber | first1 = Tomasz
 | last2 = Soja | first2 = Natalia
 | arxiv = 1005.0023
 | title = Limit theory for planar Gilbert tessellations
 | year = 2010| bibcode = 2010arXiv1005.0023S}}.</ref> or '''random crack network'''<ref name="gadk76">{{citation
 | last1 = Gray | first1 = N. H.
 | last2 = Anderson | first2 = J. B.
 | last3 = Devine | first3 = J. D.
 | last4 = Kwasnik | first4 = J. M.
 | doi = 10.1007/BF01031092
 | issue = 6
 | journal = Mathematical Geology
 | pages = 617–626
 | title = Topological properties of random crack networks
 | volume = 8
 | year = 1976| bibcode = 1976MatG....8..617G
 | s2cid = 119949515
 }}.</ref> is a mathematical model for the formation of [[mudcrack]]s, needle-like [[crystal]]s, and similar structures. It is named after [[Edgar Gilbert]], who studied this model in 1967.<ref name="g67">{{citation
 | last = Gilbert | first = E. N. | authorlink = Edgar Gilbert
 | editor-last = Noble | editor-first = B.
 | contribution = Random plane networks and needle-shaped crystals
 | location = New York
 | publisher = Macmillan
 | title = Applications of Undergraduate Mathematics in Engineering
 | year = 1967}}.</ref>

In Gilbert's model, cracks begin to form at a set of points randomly spread throughout the plane according to a [[Poisson distribution]]. Then, each crack spreads in two opposite directions along a line through the initiation point, with the slope of the line chosen uniformly at random. The cracks continue spreading at uniform speed until they reach another crack, at which point they stop, forming a T-junction. The result is a [[tessellation]] of the plane by irregular [[convex polygon]]s.

A variant of the model that has also been studied restricts the orientations of the cracks to be axis-parallel, resulting in a random tessellation of the plane by [[rectangle]]s.<ref name="mm96">{{citation
 | last1 = Mackisack | first1 = Margaret S.
 | last2 = Miles | first2 = Roger E.
 | doi = 10.2307/1428161
 | issue = 4
 | journal = Advances in Applied Probability
 | mr = 1418243
 | pages = 993–1013
 | title = Homogeneous rectangular tessellations
 | volume = 28
 | year = 1996| jstor = 1428161
 | s2cid = 121419003
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Burridge | first1 = James
 | last2 = Cowan | first2 = Richard
 | last3 = Ma | first3 = Isaac
 | arxiv = 1201.5780
 | doi = 10.1239/aap/1363354100
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Advances in Applied Probability
 | pages = 1–19
 | title = Full- and half-Gilbert tessellations with rectangular cells
 | volume = 45
 | year = 2013| s2cid = 119583382
 }}.</ref>

{{harvtxt|Gray|Anderson|Devine|Kwasnik|1976}} write that, in comparison to alternative models in which cracks may cross each other or in which cracks are formed one at a time rather than simultaneously, "most mudcrack patterns in nature topologically resemble" the Gilbert model.
